english.html: taken such kinds of substitutions sometimes as a game, and have left the deed wholly unpunished. At other times they have punished it, but very gently. Others, more severe, have punished it with civil death, and some (very few in number, however) with natural death. And so that it may not seem to the reader that I have spoken on credit, I have been willing to seek out a little further afield the more noble, illustrious and memorable examples. When Jacob, to defraud Esau his elder brother of the paternal blessing, substituted upon himself, by the counsel of Rebecca his mother, the name and person of Esau, wrapping his hands and neck in goatskins so as to show himself hairy as his brother was, and dressing himself in Esau's most precious garments, he carried off by this fraud (says Scripture) the blessing of his father Isaac, and was made lord over his brothers and plentiful in goods, to whom the peoples did reverence <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>; and thus, says St Augustine, so far was he from being reproved or punished by God for it, that he received for it reward and recompense <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. Likewise also, when Laban, having promised Rachel his younger daughter to Jacob, who had served him seven years to have Rachel, on the day of the wedding substituted in the nuptial bed Leah his elder daughter, and made her lie with Jacob, and moreover constrained him to serve another seven years to recover Rachel, God was not angered at it <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>. Laodice, wife of King Antiochus, after having killed her husband, substituted in the royal bed Artemon, feigning him to be her husband (because he wholly resembled Antiochus), so that from there he might speak to the people and commend to them his wife and his children; whereupon the people, persuaded that this commendation proceeded from Antiochus (to whom the people was devoted and most affectionate), would not afterwards elect any King without the opinion and counsel of Laodice: who by means of this cruel imposture received reward and recompense, so far was she from feeling any penalty whatever <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. notes.gloss: Artemon, a man of the people who resembled Antiochus II of Syria, put in the royal bed by the queen Laodice after she had the king killed, to commend her and her children to the people.
